text: Quantum optimization doesn't start with qubits -- it starts with an ordinary class of hard problems that businesses already pay classical solvers to chew on. Before touching a single quantum circuit, you need to recognize what these problems look like, and why their size alone makes them brutal.

Every combinatorial optimization problem has the same three ingredients. Decision variables are the things you're choosing -- is asset i in the portfolio, does the truck visit city j right after city i. An objective function is a number that scores any particular choice -- total return, total distance, total unmet demand. And constraints are rules that rule out some combinations, like a budget cap or 'visit every city exactly once.'

Here's the part that surprises people coming from continuous optimization: a finite number of choices does not make a problem small. With n binary variables, the number of candidate solutions is 2 to the n. At n equals 20, that's about one million -- still searchable on a laptop. At n equals 50, it's already past a quadrillion, far beyond brute force on any machine. And at n equals 300, a modest-sized real portfolio or routing problem, the candidate count exceeds the number of atoms estimated to exist in the observable universe.

Three business-shaped examples recur throughout this course. Portfolio selection: choose K of N assets that maximize expected return while keeping correlated risk under control -- you'll build this exact QUBO in Lesson 15. Vehicle routing, the Traveling Salesman Problem: find the stop order minimizing total distance, the canonical example in nearly every quantum optimization paper. And shift scheduling: assign workers so every shift is covered without illegal patterns, minimizing overtime cost. Every one of these reduces to the same mathematical object: a QUBO.

Next lesson defines that universal translation layer precisely: the Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization problem, or QUBO -- the one mold that QAOA, quantum annealers, and classical heuristics alike are all built to run on.
